text: Isham Warren Garrott (c. 1816 – June 17, 1863) was a colonel in the Confederate States Army during the American Civil War and was killed by a Union sharpshooter on June 17, 1863, shortly before his promotion to brigadier general was confirmed by the Confederate Senate or delivered and became effective. Born in either Anson County or Wake County, North Carolina, around 1816, Garrott graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and studied law. In 1840, he moved to Marion, Alabama, where he practiced law. He was a member of the Whig Party and a Mason, and served as an incorporator of the Marion and Alabama River Transportation Company and President of the Board of Trustees of Howard College. Garrott was elected to the Alabama House of Representatives in 1845 and 1847 and served as an elector for John C. Breckinridge's failed 1860 Presidential Election campaign. Alabama Governor Andrew B. Moore sent Garrott to North Carolina as a commissioner to enlist his home state's aid in joining the secession movement. When the Civil War began, Garrott formed the 20th Alabama Infantry Regiment, serving briefly as its lieutenant colonel from September 16, 1861, to October 7, 1861, and thereafter as its colonel. The brigade was stationed in Mobile, Alabama during 1861 and 1862, and was later sent to Mississippi as part of General Edward D. Tracy's brigade. Garrott participated in the Battle of Port Gibson and the Battle of Champion's Hill. His commission to the rank of brigadier general, dated May 28, 1863, was received at headquarters after his death, and because of his death, the posthumous appointment was not confirmed by the Confederate Senate. According to Warner's footnote, Garrott was buried under the window of a friend's (Finney) house in Vicksburg, and his remains were never moved, as noted in a letter from his wife. A Confederate undertaker's list of CS burials in Vicksburg was lost—though partially recovered years later—and reported a "Colonel Garnet" of the 20th Alabama with an unknown gravesite. It appears Garrott was reburied in Vicksburg's Cedar Hill/Confederate Cemetery, but due to a misspelling of his surname and an incorrect rank, his general commission was received after his death, leading to the reporting that his remains were not moved from the initial burial site. Consequently, the National Park Service listing for Garrott now has his correct rank and surname but no grave number. A stone cenotaph marker for him stands in Soldiers Rest Confederate Cemetery, ironically located in the Cedar Hill (Old Vicksburg City) Cemetery. Fort Garrott near Vicksburg was named in his honor. The fort did not fall to the Union Army in battle because the planned final assault on Confederate positions scheduled for July 6, 1863, was avoided due to Lieutenant General John C. Pemberton's surrender of his army to Major General Ulysses S. Grant on July 4, 1863. The Sons of Confederate Veterans Camp 764 in Marion, Alabama, is named in his honor.
